entities.name: Virius Nepotianus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Virius Nepotianus, a scion of the Constantinian dynasty, held the prestigious office of Consul of the Roman Empire in 336 CE, a distinction that positioned him within the highest echelons of the late Roman aristocracy. His significance is largely derived from his familial connections, particularly his presumed marriage to Eutropia, a daughter of Emperor Constantius I Chlorus and half-sister to Constantine the Great. This matrimonial alliance cemented his ties to the imperial household, affording him considerable influence and status during a period of intense political maneuvering and dynastic consolidation within the Tetrarchic and Constantinian eras.

Nepotianus's career trajectory saw him attain the consulship alongside Tettius Fascianus, a role that signified senatorial approval and imperial favor. While specific details of his administrative or military achievements during his consulship are sparse in surviving historical records, his elevation to this supreme magistracy indicates a trusted position within Constantine's court. The consulship in the 4th century CE, though largely ceremonial compared to its Republican antecedents, still conferred immense prestige and was often a stepping stone for individuals favored by the reigning emperor, marking them as central figures in the political landscape of the vast Roman state.

His most enduring, albeit indirect, legacy stems from his probable paternity of the usurper Nepotianus, who briefly seized Rome in 350 CE. This familial link to a short-lived, violent challenge to imperial authority under Magnentius and Constantius II, underscores the volatile nature of succession and power in the mid-4th century. While Virius Nepotianus himself remained loyal to the Constantinian line, his son's rebellion highlights the persistent undercurrents of aristocratic ambition and dynastic rivalries that continued to plague the Roman Empire, even after the consolidation of power by Constantine the Great.
